title: Guru Har Krishan: healing
hook: the eighth Guru's light: the child who served the sick
tomorrow: why would a Guru die for a faith that wasn't his own?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Har Rai: gentleness, the robe gathered close, healing for whoever asks. His son was the next Guru, and he was a child.

Baba Kartar has a cough that won't quit, and he's decided not to see a doctor. Suffering is the medicine, he says, quoting the Granth, and goes back to his tea. Harjit says he's being stubborn. Simran is caught in the middle, texting you from the hallway. And the Guru for this argument is a child. Tradition says Guru Har Krishan became Guru very young, and when he came to Delhi, sickness was moving through the city. He went among the sick and served them, caught the illness himself, and died. A hard story, told gently: he gave his short life to people who were ill.
screen: `A COUGH THAT WON'T QUIT.` → `SUFFERING IS THE MEDICINE?` → `A CHILD GURU AMONG THE SICK.`

segments.voice: Here's the line Baba Kartar quoted, from Guru Nanak in Asa di Var, Ang 469. In paraphrase: suffering is the medicine, and comfort the disease, because in comfort we forget. Readers take it two ways, and both love the line. One side says: take it as it stands. Pain teaches what comfort hides; meet it without bitterness and let it turn you toward the Name. Its best case: the line isn't about doctors at all, and someone who has learned from pain has learned something real. The other side says: read it beside the Gurus' lives. Guru Har Rai kept medicines. Guru Har Krishan, still a child, walked toward the sick. Its best case: the line is about pride and forgetting, not refusing care; accepting God's will can include accepting a doctor. What both keep is the Ardas, which remembers him like this, in paraphrase: think of Guru Har Krishan, and seeing him, all suffering goes. One to tell a friend tonight: the Sikh standing prayer remembers a child Guru as a healer. Simran doesn't win the argument. She sits with Baba Kartar and says: the child Guru went to the sick. Maybe the sick can go to the doctor. He laughs, coughs, and says he'll think about it.
screen: `SUFFERING IS THE MEDICINE.` · `ONE SIDE: MEET IT, LEARN.` · `THE OTHER: THE GURUS HEALED.` · `SEEING HIM, SUFFERING GOES.` · then, large: `HEALING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who's unwell right now, in body or in spirit. Write them a short message, just a few honest words, and leave it ready on your screen. Breathe slowly with their name in mind, and when the sit ends, decide whether to send it.
Guru Har Krishan: the eighth Guru, a child who went toward the sick. Healing, given at a cost.
Keep close: healing, the child who walked toward the sick. Baba Kartar is still thinking it over.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Har Krishan in the Ardas as the one whose sight removes suffering; Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi, linked with his stay there, is visited by many, and its sarovar water is taken home by some.

chat.meaning: Ang 469 warns that comfort makes us forget. Guru Har Rai kept medicines and Guru Har Krishan served the sick; care fits the line.
